seoDescription: Learn to build a professional chatbot user interface using Gradio for your large language model (LLM) Q&A bot. This tutorial demonstrates how to create a multi-tab Gradio application, connecting a frontend to a backend powered by Google's Flan, LangChain, and LlamaIndex (formerly GPT-Index). You'll see how to structure the UI with separate tabs for knowledge indexing and chatting, implement streaming responses for a dynamic user experience, and debug common issues within a Google Colab environment.

chapters.title: Introduction: Building a Gradio UI for an LLM Chatbot
chapters.description: This chapter introduces the project as the second part of a series, focusing on building a Gradio UI for an existing LLM chatbot.

chapters.title: Live Demo of the Final Chatbot Application
chapters.description: A demonstration of the completed Gradio chatbot application using a document about Ashton Kutcher to answer various questions.

chapters.title: Code Walkthrough: The `build_the_bot` Function
chapters.description: This section explains the Python code for the first core function, which takes user text and builds a searchable LlamaIndex.

chapters.title: Code Walkthrough: The `chat` Function with Streaming
chapters.description: An explanation of the second core function, `chat`, which queries the index and uses Python's `yield` to create a streaming response effect.

chapters.title: Designing the UI with Gradio Blocks
chapters.description: Here, the speaker walks through the Gradio Blocks code for creating the two-tab UI, including components and event handlers.

chapters.title: First Live Coding Attempt & Debugging
chapters.description: This chapter shows the first attempt to run the new UI, which fails, leading to the identification and explanation of two critical bugs.

chapters.title: Successful Second Attempt: Testing with Elon Musk
chapters.description: After fixing the bugs by using the correct input variable and making the index global, the app is re-run and successfully tested with data about Elon Musk.

chapters.title: Final Demo with Bill Gates
chapters.description: As a final confirmation that the bot is now working correctly, the speaker runs one more quick test using a document about Bill Gates.

chapters.title: Conclusion and Learning from Mistakes
chapters.description: The speaker concludes by explaining why he chose to keep his debugging process in the video and provides a final summary of the technologies used.

summary:
## Project Goal
This tutorial demonstrates how to build a dynamic, multi-tab user interface for a Large Language Model (LLM) Q&A bot using the **Gradio** library. The backend logic, which uses **Google's Flan-T5**, **LangChain**, and **LlamaIndex**, is assumed to be pre-built.

## Core Application Logic
The application is structured around two main Python functions that power the Gradio UI.

### 1. `build_the_bot(input_text)`
- **Purpose**: To process user-provided text and create a searchable knowledge base.
- **Process**:
    1. Takes a string of text (`input_text`) as input.
    2. Uses this text to create a **LlamaIndex** `Document`.
    3. Builds a `GPTSimpleVectorIndex` using the document, a pre-configured `llm_predictor` (Flan-T5), and an embedding model.
    4. Returns a confirmation message to the user, like "Indexing is successful".

### 2. `chat(user_input, chat_history)`
- **Purpose**: To handle the conversational Q&A part of the chatbot.
- **Process**:
    1. Takes the user's latest question (`user_input`) and the existing conversation (`chat_history`).
    2. Queries the previously built index with the user's input: `index.query(user_input)`.
    3. Implements a streaming response by iterating through the characters of the bot's answer and `yield`ing the updated chat history at each step.

## Gradio UI with `gr.Blocks`
The UI is constructed using **Gradio Blocks** for a customized, two-tab layout.

- **Tab 1: "Input Text Document"**
    - A large `gr.Textbox` for the user to paste their knowledge source (e.g., a Wikipedia article).
    - A `gr.Button` labeled "Build the Bot" that triggers the `build_the_bot` function.
    - An output `gr.Textbox` to display the "Indexing is successful" message.

- **Tab 2: "Knowledge Bot"**
    - A `gr.Chatbot` component to display the conversation history.
    - A `gr.Textbox` for the user to type their questions.
    - Instead of a button, the textbox's `.submit()` event is used to trigger the `chat` function, creating a more natural chat experience.

## Key Implementation & Debugging
- **Streaming Responses**: To simulate a "typing" effect like ChatGPT, the response string is split into characters. A `for` loop appends each character to a new string and `yield`s the `chat_history` and the partially built response back to the Gradio UI.
- **Event Handling**:
    - The indexing button uses the `.click()` event handler.
    - The chat input box uses the `.submit()` event handler, passing the chat history and the new message as a list of inputs `[chatbot, message]` and receiving the updated `chatbot` component as output.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Variable Scoping and State Management**: A critical bug was fixed during the demonstration. The `index` object created in `build_the_bot` was not accessible to the `chat` function. For this demo, the issue was resolved by declaring `index` as a **`global`** variable. In a production application, it's better to manage state by passing the index object or saving/loading it from a file (e.g., `index.json`).
transcription:
## Introduction: Building a Gradio UI for an LLM Chatbot

Hey, what's up, coders? Welcome to One Little Coder. In this tutorial, we're going to learn how to build a chatbot UI using a Gradio application. This is the second part of my first tutorial, where we used Google's Flan, a large language model, and LangChain and GPT Index or Llama Index to use an open-source language model to build a Q&A bot. But we left that code at Google Colab, and we did not create a UI. And a lot of people had been asking me that we should actually build a UI. So this is basically the second part of the first video. So I would strongly encourage you to watch the first video if you need to understand how this chatbot actually works. But here, we are going to build the front end, and then we are going to build the front end in such a way that it looks like a chatbot, and we are going to use one of our favorite tools, Gradio, for that.

So first, I would like to show you a quick demo of how it is going to look like. Then I'm going to take you into the code, which is also in Google Colab, and explain the chatbot part. I'm not going to explain the large language part—large language model part—where we use Flan to build the Q&A bot, but this is only going to be the front end and the Gradio pattern itself.

## Live Demo of the Final Chatbot Application

So, let me show you how the chatbot looks like. This is how it looks like. You can go here and ask any question.

So I've already pasted a document about Ashton Kutcher, so I'm going to ask a question. So, um, what are the companies where Ashton has invested? What are the companies where Ashton is invested? Okay, let's see if it mentions one or two companies. Okay, it says Virgin Galactic. Okay. What are the three companies? Let's say if it gives me more number of companies. It again gives me Virgin Galactic. So what are the startups? Let me ask a question a different way. So what are the startups where Ashton has invested? Let's see if it says something. It is ResearchGate. Okay, cool. So we have got an answer.

Okay, who is Ashton Kutcher? Who's, who is he, by the way? So he is an actor. Cool.

When was Ashton born? And let's see if it gives the right answer. Empty response. We didn't get any response. Okay, let me ask it in a different way. What is the birth date of Ashton Kutcher? And then see what happens. February 21st, 1971. Let me go to the Wikipedia and then see. February 7, 1978. That's wrong. So it has probably picked up a different date, but overall our objective is to say that this chatbot is actually working fine.

So now what we are going to do is we're going to see the code part on how to build this chatbot itself. First, let me take you to the Google Colab. So I'm going to stop this. So this is not going to work for now. But okay, let me stop it again.

## Code Walkthrough: The `build_the_bot` Function

So this is the part, like if you have seen the first video, you know we ended the code somewhere here. So we ended with index.query, and then we asked a question, and it responded. So now the rest of the part begins, where we are going to build a UI—user interface, a chatbot user interface using Gradio. Now, the first thing that you need to do is `pip install gradio`.

Once you have successfully installed Gradio, then next you need to import Gradio as `gr`. Now typically, if you have been watching our channel, you know that for Gradio, we need three important things: one is a function, second is an input, and third is an output. So typically, most of the Gradio applications that we have built on this channel had only one function, but today we are going to build two functions and with two different tabs as you have seen in the interface. You can see that we have two tabs. One is the tab where you can go paste the knowledge, the text in itself, and then ask it to build an index, and then you can ask questions with the knowledge bot. So for that, we need to have two core functions that Gradio will use to do whatever we are asking it to do.

The first function I'm calling it `build_the_bot`, and the second function I'm calling it `chat`.

## Code Walkthrough: The `chat` Function with Streaming

So what is the first function supposed to do? So the first function is going to take the input text, and then it is going to build a LlamaIndex document, and it is going to build a `GPTsimpleVectorIndex`, which is the LlamaIndex. So this index we can use now to ask questions about the chatbot. Now, again, the input text string goes here, and from that we are going to build a Llama document, and from that we are going to build the `GPTsimpleVectorIndex`. Now, the documents, `embed_model`, `llm_predictor`—all these things are predefined. So the document comes from this. The `llm_predictor` is something that we have already defined using the large language model, in this particular case, the Flan model and also the embedding model in this particular case is a Hugging Face embedding model. So these things are already predefined. So we are simply using `GPTSimpleVectorIndex` to build an index. You're not returning the index, it's just stored there as an object, but you can also store, save the index as an index.json or something and then you can load it. It's up to you, the code is already available here if you want to do that. But for now, we have built the index object and with that, we are going to return a message to the user saying, "Indexing is successful." So you can see that we have returned a message to the user saying, "Indexing is successful."

After we have done that, now we are going to build the second, second function. What is the second function? The second function is a chat function where somebody can ask a question and then it is going to respond something, but we want it to be a chat interface. And also, you know, wouldn't it be fun if we have like the streaming response like how ChatGPT does? And this is exactly what we're going to do. So the first object in this function is `chat_history`, so that is going to be always there. So you're going to receive `chat_history` and you are going to send `chat_history`. And then the next object is the `user_input`, so this is the actual question that the user is asking. Now, when the user asks the question, you are going to do `index.query` with the user input. So index has been already built. `index.query` will let you ask or query this index. So you're going to take the question from the user and do `index.query` and then get this output, and that is going to be the `bot_response`.

Now, this `bot_response` is good, it's a Llama object, Llama response object. But what we want to do is we want to kind of simulate what ChatGPT has been doing, the streaming response. And thankfully, Gradio has a very easy hack to do the streaming response, and that is exactly what I've done. So we are going to create a temporary string here called `response`, and that response is basically what we are going to use to create the streaming response. So the entire response, the `bot_response` that we got, it is a response object. From that, we are going to extract `.response`. So at this point, `bot_response.response` is a string. Now we are going to split this string by every character. Let's say I've got "how are you," h-o-w, everything is going to be a separate iterative element. So that's what we are doing here. Now we are going to iterate through every single letter in that string, which is the response that the bot has given us. And we are going to add it to `response`, and while we are doing that, we are going to return—we are going to `yield`, in this case, not return, we are going to `yield` it, so that it can be displayed to the user along with the chat history. Now that is done. Now we are going to talk about the UI design, the user interface design.

## Designing the UI with Gradio Blocks

So as you can see the Gradio application, we've got a very simple title. You have got two tabs. Inside the first tab, we have a text box where the input is collected, and then we have a text box where there's an output message is displayed, and then we have a button. In the knowledge bot tab, we have a simple chat interface at the top, but there is no button. All you have to do is type the question here, send it. Type the question, send it. So that's exactly what we are going to design.

Now, we're going to use Gradio Blocks. `gr.Blocks as demo`. We have a simple markdown here. So if you want a title, you can do title, whatever you want, `Q&A Bot with Hugging Face Models`. And we can say we want the first tab, which is `gr.Tab("Input Text Document")`. Here, they have a, you have a text input, you have a text output, and then you have a text button. Now, when you click the button, then the function this is called with this input and this output. So basically you're telling this that when the first tab, in the first tab, you're going to have three elements on the screen: an input text box, an output text box, which you cannot edit, and then a button. And when the button is clicked, the function called `build_the_bot` is going to be called with the input text, and whatever the output text is being returned by the function will be displayed in the `text_output`.

Now, the second tab is called `Knowledge Tab`. Now what do we do in the `Knowledge Tab`? We're going to build a chatbot, that's why `gr.Chatbot()`. And we are going to have a text box where you can send a message. And instead of having a button to create a chat interface, we are going to use the text box itself as a submit option. So you can submit like directly from an action from the text box in itself. And when you do that, we are going to call the function called `chat`. And instead of sending only one object, we are sending a list here, which has the chatbot, which is the chat history, and also the message, which is the user what they've typed. And we are going to get the response as chatbot again. So instead of sending a string, getting a string, we are going to send the chatbot and again get the chatbot as an output.

That's what this `yield`ing is going to do. The `chat_history` plus user input response is going to help us do. So now, at this point, all these are good and well, the UI has been designed the way we wanted. And you can see that we have got the demo, we are queuing it, and then launching it. I'm doing `debug=True` just because I wanted to see if there is any error, but if you are very sure that there is no error, you can remove that. I am going to run this and then I'm going to show you how the interface looks like.

## First Live Coding Attempt & Debugging

And then I'm going to give you a quick recap of the code. And also, this time, instead of Ashton Kutcher, we can try something. So, let's see, the code is run. I'm going to click this link. This is going to open in a new tab for me. I wanted it to be new. Q&A Bot with hugging face models. Cool, well and good. So this is the place where we can input a text box. So I'm going to go to Wikipedia and I'm going to look for somebody new. So I'm going to say Elon Musk. Okay, probably I don't know how much the bot is going to screw up, but let's see. Elon Musk. I'm going to copy all these things. It's quite a big page, honestly. It's a big page. Copy this, go to the Gradio application, in the text box paste this, and then click 'Build the Bot.'

Once you click 'Build the Bot,' it's going to take a bit of time. It took me about like 2.something seconds. Then it said, "Indexing is successful." So indexing is done. I'm going to go to the knowledge what... I'm going to ask a simple question. Click here, send the document. "What is this document about?" It's, it says Ashton Kutcher.

Is this still about Ashton Kutcher? Let me go see if there is any indexing issue.

So the reason why the result showed Ashton Kutcher is because I made two rookie mistakes. One, when I was reading this user input, you would have seen that I was using `text1`, which is wrong, I should have been using `input_text`. And the second mistake is even though that we are building an index, we are not actually making this index available globally. So we had to make this index available globally, and that's exactly why you can see that now I've made the index available globally. The right way to do it is to return it or store it as a JSON object and then retrieve it. But just because this is a demo, I'm making this index available globally. The disadvantage in this case is if you have got multiple objects with `index`, then it might mess it up. So `global` is usually not advisable to do it, but because I know for sure that I'm using only one index here, this is going to work fine. So I'm going to rerun this code.

## Successful Second Attempt: Testing with Elon Musk

Like I said, I've fixed two things. One is the text list where I'm using `input_text`, second is making it `index` globally available. So I'm going to rerun this again, this, this, and this, and let's see what is going to happen this time when I'm going to ask questions about Elon Musk. So I'm going to go click the link now once again, paste the article from Elon Musk, and then click 'Build the Bot.'

And then ideally it should say 'Index Successfully'. Go to the knowledge bot. I'm going to ask, "What is this about?" It is going to tell me Elon Musk. Maybe? No, it's his Tesla. That's fine. And then let's ask another question saying, "When was Elon Musk born?" And let's see what does it say. It's going to tell us that June 28, 1971. So let's go see if it is June 28, 1971. Okay, it's June 28, 1971. So the next question that we are going to ask is, we are going to ask, "What all the companies started by Elon Musk?" And then let's see if it answers one of the questions right, like at least like one of the companies. Okay, it says Tesla. That's fine. "Is there any other company Elon Musk started other than Tesla?" Most likely it will say yes, I think. Let's see. Okay, it says Tesla, it just said Tesla. Anyways.

## Final Demo with Bill Gates

So, we have successfully learned how to build a knowledge bot. If you still doubt the code, I would like to quickly show you one more demo. So instead of Elon Musk, let's pick somebody else. In this case, I'm going to get Bill Gates. So get Bill Gates, get everything about Bill Gates. Probably this is fine. Yeah. Copy this. Go back to the page, paste it. Click 'Build the Bot'. It is going to now create the index, save it. Go to the knowledge bot and then ask, "What is this document about?" And then let's see what it says. It says it's about Bill Gates. Okay. "Who is Bill Gates?" And it's going to say most likely Bill Gates... it says Microsoft. Okay, fine. So we have successfully learned to build a bot. You can now optimize this bot. You can use different large language model and play with it.

## Conclusion and Learning from Mistakes

But at this point, we have successfully managed to build a chatbot on top of Gradio. I did not edit out my mistake because I wanted you to know what kind of mistake can cause what kind of problems. I have kept that. If you are annoyed by that, I'm really sorry that I kept my mistake in the video. But I've heard from a lot of people who appreciate when I show my mistakes and the, like, the bugs and the errors, that how do I resolve it. And people have told me that helps, that's why I've kept it.

So, so far in this video, we learned how to build a UI, a Gradio front end for a knowledge bot that we learned to build using Flan, open source model, GPT Index, Llama Index, and also LangChain. If you have any questions, let me know in the comment section. Otherwise, see you in another video. Peace.
